info.GpuCoreOffsetMhz:
Shifts the NVIDIA GPU's whole clock-voltage curve by this amount.

Positive: more clock at the same voltage, so more performance. Too much causes artefacts or driver crashes; raise it in small steps (e.g. +50 MHz) and test.
Negative: lower clock, less power and heat.

Excludes the GPU performance curve: only one of the two applies.
info.GpuMemoryOffsetMhz:
Raises or lowers the graphics memory clock.

A higher clock means more memory bandwidth, which helps most at high resolutions. Too much causes artefacts. The memory corrects small errors itself, and then performance drops despite the higher clock. Check with a benchmark after each step that it really gets faster.
info.GpuVfCurve:
Sets a clock for each voltage point of the NVIDIA GPU, like the curve editor in MSI Afterburner.

The usual use is undervolting: the same clock at a lower voltage. The GPU runs cooler and quieter and often holds its boost longer, so equal or better performance. Too little voltage for a clock crashes games.

Replaces the GPU clock offset.
info.MaxFan:
Runs both fans at full speed all the time (HP BIOS function).

Best cooling and therefore the highest sustained clocks, but very loud. When off, the fan curve or the BIOS controls the fans again.
info.GpuUnleashed:
Unlocks the raised GPU power limit and NVIDIA Dynamic Boost through the HP BIOS, like the OMEN Gaming Hub's Unleashed mode.

The GPU may draw more watts and also borrows power from the CPU budget when the CPU does not need it (115 W measured on this device). More FPS in games, at the cost of more heat and fan noise.
info.CpuTemperatureLimitC:
Maximum CPU temperature (Tctl). When the CPU reaches it, it lowers its clock.

Lower: cooler and quieter, but less performance under sustained load.
Higher: more performance, but a warmer chassis. 60 to 95 °C are allowed.
info.CpuStapmLimitMw:
Long-term CPU power limit (Skin Temperature Aware Power Management). It applies to the average over several minutes and keeps the chassis from overheating.

Higher: more sustained performance for long loads such as rendering or compiling.
Lower: cooler and quieter under sustained load.

Set through the HP BIOS and accepted in whole watts only. The lowest of the three power limits always wins.
info.CpuSlowPptLimitMw:
Medium-term CPU power limit, averaged over a few seconds up to about a minute. It decides how long the CPU may keep drawing a lot of power after a short boost.

Higher: loads such as game loading screens or short exports stay at high clocks for longer.
Lower: the clock drops sooner after a boost.

Set through the HP BIOS and accepted in whole watts only.
info.CpuPptLimitMw:
Short-term CPU power limit (Package Power Tracking): the peak power the CPU may draw for short boosts.

Higher: snappier response and higher peak clocks.
Lower: fewer heat spikes and fan jumps.

Over longer periods the slow and STAPM limits cap power as well.
info.CpuTdcMa:
Sustained current limit of the CPU power supply in amperes (Thermal Design Current).

Lower: voltage regulators and CPU stay cooler, sustained performance drops.
Higher: more sustained performance as long as cooling keeps up. 108 A is this CPU's factory maximum.
info.CpuEdcMa:
Peak current limit of the CPU in amperes (Electrical Design Current) for very short load spikes.

Too low: the clock collapses during load spikes.
Higher: higher boost clocks under short loads.
info.CpuPboScalar:
Precision Boost Overdrive scalar (1x to 10x). Lets the CPU boost with a higher voltage for longer.

Can extend the boost a little but costs noticeably more voltage and heat. On laptops it rarely brings measurable gains. 1 is the default.
info.CpuBoostProfile:
Chooses how early and how strongly the CPU clocks up.

Power saver: clocks up cautiously, cooler and more efficient.
Performance: clocks up quickly and feels snappier.
Automatic: default behaviour.
info.CpuCurveOptimizerAllCore:
Shifts the voltage curve of all CPU cores. One step is roughly 3 to 5 mV.

Negative (undervolting): less voltage for the same clock, so cooler, more efficient and often higher boost clocks.
Too negative: crashes or errors, often only at idle or light load.

Change it in small steps and check with a stress test and normal use.
info.CpuCurveOptimizerPerCore:
Like Curve Optimizer for all cores, but for each core separately.

A CPU's fastest cores usually tolerate less undervolting than the rest. Per-core values get more out of the CPU without making the best cores unstable.
info.CpuAllCoreVoltageOffsetMv:
Fixed voltage offset in millivolts for all cores.

Negative: cooler and more efficient. Too negative: crashes. Unlike Curve Optimizer, the offset applies equally to every clock step.
info.AmdCpuVoltageMv:
Fixed CPU voltage in millivolts for manual overclocking.

Disables automatic voltage control. Too high harms the CPU over time, too low causes crashes. Only useful together with a fixed clock.
info.AmdCpuClockMhz:
Fixed clock for all cores in MHz.

Disables automatic boost: steady performance, but single cores no longer reach their highest boost clocks.
info.IntelPl1Mw: Intel CPUs: long-term power limit (Power Limit 1). Sets sustained performance under long loads.
info.IntelPl2Mw: Intel CPUs: short-term power limit (Power Limit 2). Sets how much power the CPU may draw for a few seconds after a load starts.
info.IntelPl4Mw: Intel CPUs: absolute peak power (Power Limit 4) that is never exceeded.
info.IntelIccMaxMa: Intel CPUs: the highest current the CPU may draw. Too low limits boost.
info.IntelCpuPowerBalance: Intel CPUs: how the power budget is weighted between CPU cores and integrated graphics.
info.IntelCacheVoltageOffsetMv: Intel CPUs: voltage offset for the cache in millivolts. Negative saves power, too negative causes crashes.
info.IntelSystemAgentVoltageOffsetMv: Intel CPUs: voltage offset for the system agent (memory controller and I/O) in millivolts.
info.IntelCoreRatios: Intel CPUs: turbo multipliers by number of active cores, comma separated (e.g. 48, 47, 46). Clock = multiplier × 100 MHz.
info.WindowsBoostMode:
Boost mode of the Windows power plan.

Disabled: no boost above base clock. Much cooler and quieter, but clearly slower.
Enabled / Aggressive: Windows lets the CPU boost, Aggressive as often as possible.
Efficient: boosts only when it is worth the energy.
info.WindowsMinimumProcessorPercent:
Lowest performance state Windows allows the CPU, in percent.

Higher: faster response, but more idle power. Low (5 %) is the default.
info.WindowsMaximumProcessorPercent:
Highest performance state Windows allows the CPU, in percent.

100 % allows full boost. Even 99 % practically disables boost: cool and quiet, but slower.
info.WindowsProcessorEppPercent:
Energy Performance Preference: how quickly the CPU clocks up.

0 %: full performance immediately.
100 %: as efficient as possible.
Values in between are a compromise; 50 % is balanced.
info.WindowsCoreParkingMinPercent:
Share of cores Windows keeps active at least.

100 %: no core is parked. Lower latency, more idle power.
Low: unused cores sleep and save power.
info.WindowsCoreParkingMaxPercent: Share of cores Windows uses at most at the same time. Below 100 %, cores stay parked even under load: more efficient, but slower in multi-core loads.
info.CpuCcdAffinity:
Chooses which core complex (CCD) the program in the foreground runs on: 1 = first CCD, 2 = second CCD, 3 = both (Windows schedules freely).

The Omen Hub++ background service applies this to every program that comes to the foreground and gives all of them their old assignment back once 3 applies again. Keeping games on one CCD can lower latency but halves the available cores. Protected programs (for example with anti-cheat) may refuse the change.
info.WindowsEnergyMode:
The power mode from Windows Settings (System > Power).

Best performance: Windows prefers high clocks.
Best power efficiency: Windows slows background work and clocks.
info.WindowsPowerPlan: Chooses the active Windows power plan. High performance keeps clocks and voltage higher, power saver lowers consumption and performance.
info.DisplayRefreshRateHz:
Refresh rate of the built-in display in Hz.

Higher: smoother motion.
Lower (e.g. 60 Hz): saves noticeable power on battery.
info.GraphicsMode:
Display output switch (MUX).

Hybrid: the integrated graphics drive the display and the NVIDIA GPU renders only when needed. Efficient on battery.
NVIDIA GPU only: the NVIDIA GPU is wired directly to the display. More FPS and lower latency, but higher power draw.
Integrated GPU only: NVIDIA GPU off, longest battery life.

Takes effect after a restart.

info.mode:
Chooses the laptop's performance mode as in OMEN Gaming Hub. Omen Hub++ sends the same BIOS commands itself, without HP services.

Quiet: quietest Balanced step. CPU sustained power 55 W, Dynamic Boost off on AC.
Balanced: default. CPU sustained power 55 W, Dynamic Boost on.
Performance: more performance. CPU sustained power 60 W, GPU with cTGP and Dynamic Boost.
Unleashed: maximum, AC only. CPU sustained power 80 W, shared CPU+GPU budget 72 W.

The BIOS cannot report the mode itself; GPU switches and the CPU limit are checked. If anything fails, Omen Hub++ restores Balanced.

curve.help:
GPU curve
Drag: move a point or the selected range vertically.
Shift + drag point: move the loaded base curve/selection.
Alt + drag point: move the current draft/selection evenly.
Ctrl + drag point: tilt the curve around the opposite end point.
Shift + drag in empty chart: select a voltage range.
Shift + Left/Right: extend the selection. Ctrl + A: all points.
Shift + Enter: flatten the selection; without one, plateau from the point.
Esc or double-click: clear the selection; Esc while dragging: cancel.

Common controls
Left/Right: choose a point. Up/Down: 1 MHz or 1 %.
Ctrl + Up/Down: 10 steps. Enter: edit the number field.
Ctrl + Z: undo. Ctrl + Y / Ctrl + Shift + Z: redo.
Ctrl + D: reset to the loaded draft. Ctrl + S: save profile.
Mouse wheel or +/−: zoom voltage/temperature. Ctrl: Y axis.
Shift + mouse wheel: scroll horizontally. Ctrl + 0: whole curve.

Fans
Ctrl + Left/Right: edit temperature. Shift: larger steps.
Right-click: add or delete a point. Ins: add point. Del: remove point.
One shared curve applies to CPU and GPU fans; saving hands it to the fan service.

The GPU curve is applied through a preset.
Fixed voltage/clock lock and OC Scanner are not available yet.
